parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A woman reports a lost bag to a bus company.
script: Metro Buses customer service, Liam speaking.
Hello. I left my bag on one of your buses this morning and I'm hoping someone has handed it in.
I'm sorry to hear that. Let me take some details. Which route were you on?
The number 47, from the hospital to the city centre.
And roughly what time did you get off?
About twenty past eight. I got off at the stop outside the library.
OK. Can you describe the bag?
It's a small backpack, dark green, made of canvas, with a leather strap on the top.
Any name or label on it?
No name, but there's a badge on the front pocket with a picture of a mountain. I got it on holiday.
That's helpful. And what was inside?
My laptop, which is the main thing I'm worried about, a blue umbrella, and a notebook. Oh, and my reading glasses, in a black case.
Was there any money or bank cards?
No, luckily my purse was in my coat pocket.
Good. Now, nothing matching that has been reported yet, but drivers hand in items at the end of their shift. Can I take your name?

Thank you. If the bag is handed in, you'll need to collect it from our depot on Harbour Road. It's open until 7 pm on weekdays. Bring some photo ID, and you'll also need to tell us the password on the laptop or show a receipt, so we can check it's yours.
I can do that. Is there a reference number?

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A manager welcomes new volunteers at a community garden.
script: Hi everyone, and welcome to Oakfield Community Garden. I'm Rosa, the garden manager. Thanks for volunteering with us.

A little background first. The garden was created eight years ago on land that used to be a car park. The council still owns the land, but the garden is run entirely by a charity, and almost all our work is done by volunteers like you.
Most of the food we grow goes to a local food bank. Some of it is also used in our free cookery classes for families, which take place on Thursday evenings in the community hall.
Volunteer sessions run on Tuesday and Saturday mornings. You don't need to come every week, but please sign in at the shed each time, because we need to know who is on site in case of an emergency.
Gloves and tools are provided, but please bring your own water bottle, as we don't have drinking water on site. And wear sturdy shoes, not sandals.
One more thing: we never use chemical pesticides here. If you see a problem with insects, tell one of the team leaders rather than trying to deal with it yourself.

Now, the different areas. As you come in through the gate, the tool shed is straight in front of you. To the left of the shed are the vegetable beds, which take up most of the garden. The fruit trees are along the back wall, at the far end, where they get the most sun.

On the right of the entrance there's the greenhouse, where we grow seedlings in spring. Next to the greenhouse are the compost bins, so we can carry waste plants there easily. And finally, the wildlife pond is in the far right-hand corner, behind the greenhouse. Please keep children away from the pond unless an adult is with them.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two students, Hana and Marco, and their lecturer discuss a survey about cycling to college.
script: So, Hana and Marco, tell me about your survey on cycling.
We asked students why they do or don't cycle to college. We got 312 responses, which was more than we expected.
Very good. How did you get so many?
We offered a prize draw for a free bike service. That made a big difference.
Well, we assumed bad weather would be the main reason people don't cycle. But actually, the most common answer was safety: people are worried about the traffic on the main road into college.
Weather was second, and lack of somewhere secure to leave a bike was third.
Interesting. Did anything else surprise you?
How many students said they would cycle if they could borrow a bike. Almost forty per cent.
So what will you recommend in your report?
Our main recommendation is a separate cycle lane on the main road. But that's the council's decision, so we'll also suggest things the college could do itself, like more covered bike racks.
And a bike-sharing scheme. Another college nearby has one, and it's very popular.
What are you going to do next?
I'll finish the charts this week. Marco's going to contact the other college about their scheme.
Then we'll both write the conclusion together.
One suggestion: include some quotes from the open questions. Numbers are useful, but students' own words can be very persuasive.
Good idea. We have lots of comments.
And please keep the report to two thousand words. Last year's groups often wrote far too much.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A talk about how memory works and how to study effectively.
script: Today I'd like to talk about memory, and in particular what research tells us about studying effectively.

Many students study by reading their notes again and again. It feels productive, because the material becomes familiar. But familiarity is not the same as memory. Studies consistently show that re-reading is one of the least effective ways to learn.

Far more effective is what psychologists call retrieval practice: testing yourself, for example with flashcards or practice questions, before you feel ready. The effort of trying to remember strengthens the memory, even when you get the answer wrong.

A second technique is spacing. If you have five hours to study a topic, it is much better to spread them over five days than to study for five hours the night before an exam. Cramming may help you pass the next day, but most of the information is forgotten within a week.

Third, there's sleep. During sleep, the brain replays and organises what we learned during the day. Students who stay up all night studying often remember less than those who study less but sleep properly.

What about multitasking? Many students believe they can study well while checking their phones. The research is clear that switching between tasks has a cost. Even having a phone on the desk, switched off, can reduce performance, probably because part of our attention is still on it.

Finally, a word about learning styles. You may have been told that you are a visual or an auditory learner, and that you should study in that way. There is very little evidence for this. Most people learn best when information is presented in more than one form, for example words combined with diagrams.
So, to sum up: test yourself, spread out your study, sleep well, put your phone in another room, and don't worry about your learning style.

paras: Routine appointments with a doctor can be booked up to four weeks ahead, online or by phone. Phone lines open at 8 am and are busiest in the first hour.

passages.title: Thornbury Hotels: holiday leave for staff
paras: Full-time staff are entitled to 28 days of paid holiday a year, including public holidays. Part-time staff receive the same entitlement in proportion to the hours they work.
The holiday year runs from 1 April to 31 March. Up to five unused days may be carried over to the next year, but they must be taken by the end of June.
Holiday requests should be made through the staff app at least two weeks in advance, or four weeks in advance for periods of more than one week.

Because the hotel is busiest in July and August, no more than two members of each department may be on holiday at the same time during these months. Requests are approved in the order they are received.
Staff who are ill during a holiday may be able to take the holiday again later, but only if they provide a note from a doctor.
When you leave the company, you will be paid for any holiday you have earned but not taken.

passages.title: Tips for writing a CV
paras: A  Employers often spend less than a minute on each CV, so put the most important information at the top. A short personal statement of three or four lines, explaining what you offer and what kind of job you are looking for, is a good start.

B  For each job you have had, do not simply list your duties. Describe what you achieved, using numbers where possible: 'reduced waiting times by 20%' is more convincing than 'responsible for customer service'.
C  Send a different CV for each application. Read the job advertisement carefully and make sure the skills it mentions appear clearly in your CV, using the same words where it is honest to do so.
D  Two pages is usually enough. Remove old or irrelevant jobs, and do not include a photograph, your date of birth or your marital status unless the employer asks for them.
E  Spelling mistakes create a poor impression. Ask a friend to read your CV, or read it aloud yourself, which makes errors easier to spot.
F  Finally, keep your CV up to date. Add new skills and achievements as they happen, so that you are ready when an opportunity appears.

passages.title: The quiet revolution of the electric bicycle
paras: A  When electric bicycles first appeared in significant numbers in the 1990s, they were heavy, slow and unreliable. Their lead-acid batteries weighed as much as the bicycle itself and lasted only a few hundred charges. Few people outside China took them seriously.

B  The turning point came with the lithium-ion battery, developed for laptops and mobile phones. As prices fell in the 2000s, manufacturers could build e-bikes that were light enough to look and feel like ordinary bicycles, with a range of fifty kilometres or more on a single charge. Today, in countries such as the Netherlands and Germany, more than half of all new bicycles sold are electric.

C  The appeal is not hard to understand. An e-bike does not ride itself: in most countries the motor only helps while the rider is pedalling and stops assisting above 25 kilometres per hour. But it makes hills and headwinds manageable and allows riders to arrive at work without needing a shower. Surveys show that e-bike owners cycle further and more often than owners of ordinary bicycles, and many use their e-bike to replace car journeys.

D  There are clear benefits for health, too. Critics once argued that e-bikes were a form of cheating that would make people less fit. Research has not supported this. Because e-bike riders travel more often and for longer, their total physical activity is similar to that of conventional cyclists, and much higher than that of people who drive.

E  E-bikes also raise new concerns. They are heavier and faster than ordinary bicycles, and in several countries the number of serious accidents involving older riders has risen. Battery fires, often caused by cheap or poorly maintained chargers, have led some landlords to ban e-bikes from apartment buildings. And theft is a serious problem: an e-bike can cost several thousand pounds, making it an attractive target.

F  Transport planners increasingly see the e-bike as a way to reduce traffic and emissions, especially for journeys of between five and fifteen kilometres, which are too long for most people to cycle comfortably on an ordinary bike but often made by car. Some cities now offer grants towards the cost of an e-bike, and employers in several countries can provide them to staff through tax-free schemes. Whether e-bikes reach their potential, however, will depend on whether cities build safe, separate cycle lanes.
